about: Scene patterns drawn from real political lives. Real lives calibrate only: no real name, words or event ships. Roles and settings are slots the director fills from the world's records. Gates are yes-or-no facts that may gate; weights are amounts that only weight the pick. unlocks, extends and mergesWith hold pattern ids (A = bank 1, B = bank 2, C = bank 3), kind: (a scene kind the game has today), class: (a row in docs/design/scenes/scene-catalog), later: (a kind the inventory marks needed later). Bank 3 patterns also carry alsoStages (other stages where their gates can hold; stage is the home tab) and needs (mechanics they lean on that the game lacks or only partly has, keyed to the needs list). No pattern is locked to one stage: the director may blend parts of several patterns that fit the same player into one scene (mergesWith).

stages.name: Election night
stages.about: The count, the call and the speech.

stages.name: The morning after
stages.about: Between the result and the oath.

stages.name: The first days
stages.about: The oath and the first weeks: the first vote, the first deal, the first crisis, the first test.

stages.name: The first term
stages.about: The rest of the first term.

stages.name: Governing
stages.about: The work of the office in any term: vetoes, deciding votes, deals, the rules, leadership posts, investigations, family and staff on the inside.

stages.name: Crises and scandals
stages.about: Disasters, attacks, secrets, prosecutors, illness and impeachment, in any term.

stages.name: Running again
stages.about: Re-election and what comes with it: a challenger from your own side, the party leader's word, a recall, a party switch, a run for something bigger, a running mate.

stages.name: Losing and leaving
stages.about: Refusing a loss, losing at home, stepping aside, resigning, the last weeks, a post that falls through.

stages.name: After office
stages.about: The work between races, the comeback, crossing over, a cause carried out, and old allies who become rivals.

patterns.title: Brushed off by the body

roles.fill: a problem on record that touches your home or street and that {the body} can act on
the place's own council, board or commission, by its own name
whoever chairs {the body}, by the title the place uses
the member for your district, said with how long they have held the seat

setting.text: the public comment period of {the body}'s meeting, because the turn at the microphone is the moment.

gates: Not in office.
{the problem} is on record and {the body} has the power to act on it.
A meeting with public comment is on the calendar.
weights: How much {the problem} has cost your household.

branches.then: A member moves to fix it and it passes. You are known as the one who got it done, a fact the filing scenes read.
{presiding officer} knows your name before you reach the microphone, and {district member} becomes the incumbent you would face.

branches.when: your job is covering {the body} for {outlet}
branches.then: You know the file better than the members, and speaking up puts your job's neutrality at stake.
That night {household member} asks whether you mean to do something about it.

sources.life: In 1988, as a private citizen, he told the Brooklyn Park, Minnesota, council about storm runoff piped into a wetland and felt brushed off. He ran for mayor in 1990 and beat an 18-year incumbent.
He emailed Somerville, Massachusetts, council members after each crash at the corner by his apartment until the city added a turn arrow in 2025, then ran for the council that year.

patterns.moment: You speak about {the problem} during public comment and {district member} brushes you off in front of {presiding officer}.
choices: press with what happened and who was hurt
ask who can act on it and when
say you will come back with neighbors
after a dismissive answer only: say the seat needs someone who listens
patterns.ifNo: Leaving without answering writes that you let it go. A neighbor who was there can bring it up later.

patterns.title: The seat comes to you

roles.fill: the official who runs the place's elections, by the title the place uses
a seat on {the body} that drew fewer candidates than openings

setting.text: Where {clerk} reaches you the day after the count, or the counting room if you worked the polls.

gates: Not in office.
Fewer candidates filed than seats were open.
Write-in votes for you are on the count.
weights: How many people in town know you.
Traits that feel a duty to serve.
Earlier asks to run that you turned down.

branches.then: You hear your own name read again and again, and the other counters look at you before {clerk} says a word.
{household member} reminds you that you swore off this kind of thing, or tells you to take it.

branches.when: you meant to run and missed the deadline
branches.then: A friend offers to print stickers and postcards, and the write-in becomes your own campaign.

sources.life: In 2022 in Boonsboro, Maryland, two candidates filed for three council seats. Counting ballots on the election board, he kept hearing his own name, won the third seat on write-ins, and accepted it.
He missed the ballot deadline in Winooski, Vermont, and won a council seat as a write-in with stickers, posters and postcards.

patterns.moment: Fewer people filed than there were seats, and enough voters wrote you in that {clerk} has to ask whether you will take {open seat}.
choices: ask for a day to talk it over at home
patterns.ifNo: A decline writes that you turned the seat down. {the body} fills it another way, and whoever gets it knows you could have had it.

patterns.title: Turned away from voting

roles.fill: the poll worker or deputy clerk at the table, said with the job
whoever came with you: a parent, grandparent, partner or neighbor

setting.text: the polling place or the clerk's registration counter, because the rule is applied there.

gates: Old enough to vote.
A voting rule in your state (ID, a roll purge, a moved polling place) that a fact of your household does not meet, such as a recent move or a name change.
Election day or a registration deadline.
weights: How strongly you hold views on the race.

branches.when: it is an older relative who is turned away
branches.then: She asks you to drive her to {clerk}'s office, and whether she votes depends on you.
You must turn a neighbor away under the rule: follow it, offer the provisional ballot, or call {clerk}.
Your employer brings it up at work the next day, and your job is at stake for speaking out.

sources.life: In 1962 the Mississippi sharecropper went with others to register, was failed on the literacy test and was fired by her boss for trying. She went on to help found the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party.

patterns.moment: {poll worker} tells you, or {close tie} beside you, that a voting rule on record means no ordinary ballot today.
choices: ask to see the rule in writing
go to {clerk}'s office before the polls close
patterns.ifNo: Leaving writes that you did not vote this time and why. Someone outside saw you walk out.

patterns.title: The speaker who never came

roles.fill: a candidate you back, named with the seat
whoever runs the gathering, named with the group
the friend who brought you

setting.text: Wherever the gathering is: a candidates' night, a rally, a club meeting, from the calendar.

gates: You attended the gathering.
You back one of the candidates.
weights: Speaking traits, and a school record of debate or speeches.

branches.then: {candidate} finds you after and asks you to work on the campaign full time.
The parts you pick do not fit the room. {candidate} thanks you politely, and {host} remembers you tried.
{friend} volunteers you out loud. You can still decline, and {friend} brings it up later.

sources.life: As a college student in 1930 he campaigned for Welly Hopkins, a state senate candidate, after a rousing speech at a political meeting in Blanco, Texas. Hopkins and Johnson's father then recommended him to a new congressman, who hired him. The speaker who fails to come is the game's addition.

patterns.moment: The person meant to speak for {candidate} at the gathering has not come, and the room looks for someone.
choices: stand up and speak for {candidate} (a short speech, one part at a time)
patterns.ifNo: Staying seated writes nothing against you. Someone else speaks, and an aide hands you flyers, a smaller door into the campaign.

patterns.title: The party asks you to run

roles.fill: a party official, said with the post and how they know you or your family
a seat the party does not hold, or an open county or town seat

setting.text: Where {recruiter} would reach you: a letter or call where you live now, your home, or your shop or job near closing.

gates: Not in office.
You are a party member or lean to the party.
{open seat} is on the next ballot.
weights: Credentials the party values (service, a law degree, a business).
How far your stances are from the incumbent's.
How many times in a row the party has lost the seat.

branches.when: your business or job is failing
branches.then: The ask arrives with the debts on the counter, and the backing comes with a price you name or refuse.
{household member} turns them down and they turn to you. {household member} is stung at being passed over, or relieved, by their traits.
Saying yes means moving home to meet the residency rule, and the talk at home is about the move as much as the race.
Someone else was asked first. A rival brings it up later, and {recruiter} admits it if asked.
A sit-down with the committee follows, and each answer goes on your record as a stance.

sources.life: In 1945 a Republican committee in a California district held by the same Democrat looked for a candidate. A banker and family friend wrote to Nixon, then a Navy officer, who flew out, met the committee and won the seat in 1946.

In 1922, with his clothing store failing, the Pendergast organization recruited him for county judge, an office that ran county business. He won narrowly and lost in 1924 when a rival faction backed the Republicans.
In 1975 Austin Democrats asked her husband David to run for county commissioner. He said no, so they asked her, and she won.

patterns.moment: {recruiter} asks you to run for {open seat}, and what they want back is part of the ask.
choices: ask what they would put behind you, and what it costs once you hold the seat
ask for time to talk it over at home
patterns.ifNo: A no writes that you turned the party down. The party runs someone else, and the next ask comes with less patience or from someone closer.

patterns.title: The regulars want a slate

roles.fill: someone who comes in often, named with their own work

setting.text: Your workplace, wherever your job record puts you with the public: a shop, a counter, a garage.

gates: Not in office.
Your job record puts you where the public comes in.
An election with more than one open seat on {the body} is coming.
weights: How many regulars you have ties with.
Your household's income and line of work.

branches.then: Hosting the meetings costs you customers who back the other side, and the lost business shows up later.
Your boss says no politics on the clock. Joining means meeting somewhere else, or risking the job.
{household member} offers to write the flyers and coach your speeches, which widens the speech parts you can pick.

sources.life: He ran a tailor shop in Greeneville, Tennessee, where locals argued politics while he worked. In 1829 he and friends put up a ticket of working men and he was elected to the town board.

patterns.moment: {regular} says the people who gather at your work should run their own slate for {the body}, with you on it.
choices: join the slate as a candidate
offer the place to meet but stay off the ballot
patterns.ifNo: Keeping politics out writes that you stayed out. The slate forms without you, and if it wins, its members come asking for your support on their first vote.

patterns.title: A neighbor starts a recall

roles.fill: someone {the decision} hurt the way it hurt you: another parent, a neighbor, a coworker
a local officeholder the place's law lets voters recall: a school board member, a council member, a sheriff
a decision on record by {officeholder} that touched your household

setting.text: Where people {the decision} hurt would run into each other.

gates: Not in office.
{the decision} is on record and touched your household.
The place's law allows a recall of {officeholder}.
weights: How much {the decision} cost your household.
Your ties with others it hurt.

branches.when: a child of yours is in the schools and {officeholder} sits on the school board
branches.then: {neighbor} is another parent, met at pickup, and the fight is over what the board did to your child's school.

branches.when: a seasoned campaigner offers money and know-how
branches.then: His price is a say in what the recall says, which changes who it answers to.

branches.when: many families speak another language at home
branches.then: A neighbor offers to gather signatures in it, which reaches voters the campaign could not.

branches.when: you work for the body {officeholder} sits on
branches.then: The recall is aimed at your employer, and {neighbor} wants you inside it.

sources.life: In 2021 two San Francisco parents with no political experience started a recall of school board members. A housing activist brought fundraising know-how, and in 2022 voters recalled three members.

patterns.moment: {neighbor} wants to lead a recall of {officeholder} over {the decision}, and wants you beside them.
choices: sign the petition and no more
say you would rather run for the seat at the next election
patterns.ifNo: Saying no writes that you stayed out. They run it anyway, and if it qualifies they ask again with {officeholder}'s name on every lawn sign.

patterns.title: Your neighbors pick a leader

roles.fill: a group on record you belong to: a volunteer fire company, a union local, a parents' group, a congregation committee, a neighborhood association
a member of {local group}, named with the group

setting.text: {local group}'s meeting, because the nomination happens in the room.

You belong to {local group} and its leader post is open.

branches.when: the group must take a side
branches.then: Soon it has to back or oppose a ballot measure or a candidate, and as its leader you speak for it.
The vote is by hands, and the loser is someone you see every week.

branches.when: only your own street backs you
branches.then: The tally shows where your support lives, which a later race reads.

sources.life: In 1832, about a year after moving to New Salem, Illinois, his neighbors elected him captain of their militia company. He lost his legislative race that year but carried New Salem almost to a man.

patterns.moment: At {local group}'s meeting, {member} nominates you out loud to lead it.
choices: accept only if someone you trust takes the second spot
patterns.ifNo: A decline writes that you passed. Whoever takes it leads, and the next scene that needs a local leader goes to them.

a group on record that recruits candidates
a sibling or friend who knows your views and did not tell you
a long-serving member of your own party

setting.text: Where the call finds you: at work, at home.

{cause group} is active in your area.
A recorded tie with {close tie}.
Your stances differ from {incumbent}'s on a question the group cares about.

A recent cause or protest you took part in.

branches.then: You campaign around your shifts, and customers start to recognize you.

branches.then: They are stunned you are taking it seriously. Their help depends on how you tell them.
Signing its platform writes each stance to your record, and {incumbent} quotes it.

sources.life: After the 2016 election her brother nominated her to Brand New Congress, a group recruiting outsiders. She campaigned while working at a restaurant and beat a senior incumbent in the 2018 primary though heavily outspent.

choices: take a meeting with the group
ask {close tie} why they did it before you answer
patterns.ifNo: A decline writes that the group asked and you refused. It backs someone else against {incumbent}, who later asks for your endorsement.

roles.fill: a teacher, coach or first boss the record ties to you
a government job you could not get alone: on a member's staff, in a department, on a police force

setting.text: Where {mentor} would reach you: a call home, a chance meeting at a school event.

A mentor tie with someone now in politics.
You need work or money for school.

branches.then: The office loses your paperwork. {mentor} calls a second time, and the job comes with a debt you both carry.
Under pressure in the job, you think about leaving, and {mentor} says you will regret it.

sources.life: His high school government teacher and boxing coach, Mike O'Callaghan, called a congressman to insist on a promised job when it fell through; Reid got a police job that helped pay for law school.

choices: turn it down and get there on your own
ask for a different kind of help, such as a reference
patterns.ifNo: Turning it down writes that you refused a favor. {mentor} respects it or is hurt, by the tie, and stays in your life.

patterns.title: A relative takes up a cause

roles.fill: an older relative or neighbor, named with how they are related to you
a public question on record with a group pushing it
something public and hard that the record lets them do: a long march, a fast, a sit-in, a vigil

setting.text: Wherever they would tell family first.

gates: A recorded tie with {close tie}, whose stance on {the cause} is on record.
A cause group is active on {the cause}.
weights: How strongly {close tie} holds the stance.

branches.then: Days on the road with them put you next to the cause group's organizers and in the papers, and both become ties and records.
A hospital two towns away calls, and you decide whether to end it.

branches.then: They ask you to help, which opens the relative's race.

sources.life: At 88, in 1999, she set out from Pasadena to walk to Washington for campaign finance reform, about 3,200 miles over 14 months. In 2004, at 94, she ran for the U.S. Senate in New Hampshire on small donations and lost.

patterns.moment: {close tie} tells you they are about to do {the public act} for {the cause}.
choices: join them for the first part
help from behind: drive, organize, raise money
try to talk them out of it
promise to be there at the end
patterns.ifNo: Trying to talk them out of it writes that you opposed it. They go anyway, the press follows, and a reporter asks you why you did not.

patterns.title: The last day to file

roles.fill: a friend or adviser, said with how they know you
a seat on the ballot, from the filing calendar

setting.text: Wherever the day finds you; filing itself happens at {clerk}'s counter.

gates: Not in office.
It is the last filing day for {open seat}.
A reason on record you have weighed running: a fight with {the body}, an ask you have not answered.
weights: How bad the fight with {the body} was.
How many people in town know you.

branches.when: a fact on your record backs an attack
branches.then: The incumbent says you cannot be reached (an unlisted number, a second home), and you answer it at the first forum.
The party's candidate just dropped out, and {party official} calls to ask you to fill the line before closing.

sources.life: After fighting the Carmel, California, council over a building on his property, he decided to run for mayor hours before the 1986 filing deadline. The incumbent attacked his unlisted phone number, and he won in a landslide.

the local party leader, said with years in the post
someone who has worked the district for decades, said with what they did before

setting.text: Wherever the party meets in this place, from its records: a back room, a hall, an office.

You are registered with or lean to {party}.
A local {party} meeting is on the calendar.

branches.then: Before you go, a parent says these are not your kind of people. Answering that you mean to help run things goes on your record as a stance.
The scoff runs the other way: a relative says those people do not want anyone like you.

sources.life: Around 1880, out of Harvard, he joined his district's Republican association, which met in a room over a saloon. His well-off friends laughed; he kept going, and his first ally was Joe Murray, who knew the district.

ask {old hand} how things work here
patterns.ifNo: Not going writes that you were invited and stayed home. Whoever asked you notices.

Party member.
Your precinct's committee seat is empty, or its holder skips the meetings.

Volunteers from each party ask you to register and file, and choosing writes your party.

choices: ask what it takes before you decide
patterns.ifNo: A no writes that you passed. Whoever files later votes on whether you get the party's backing, or on a vacancy the party fills.

Half work the polls and half quit, and the ones who quit blame you.

keep the house running and stay out of the campaign
tell them it is a mistake, or ask why now

send {visitor} to someone else on the staff

{appointer} asks how you will vote on a permit they care about, and the answer shows what you will trade.

counter with a demand of your own

change it to win over the opponents

sources.life: On primary day in 1962 a cousin warned that something was wrong in Quitman County, Georgia. A friend saw the county boss telling voters how to vote; a judge later threw out the county's ballots, and Carter won his state senate seat.

patterns.ifNo: Letting it go writes that you did not challenge. {chair} stays in charge, and if you run again the same county waits for you.

go to {party official} first and ask for a blessing
patterns.ifNo: Declining writes that you stayed loyal. The leader's pick is nominated, and {old hand}'s tie with you drops.

The other party fields no one in the special election, and you must win a full term months later.

sources.life: In 1940 her husband, Congressman Clyde Smith of Maine, ill after a heart attack, asked her to run for his seat. He died weeks later, and she won the special election.
In 1987 Congresswoman Sala Burton, dying, asked that Pelosi succeed her. Pelosi won the special election.
In 1964 the assemblyman whose club she worked in took a judgeship. The club hesitated to back her, so she went to women voters through a group she led and won.

patterns.moment: {patron} is leaving {the seat} and you want it, before or against the people who usually decide.
choices: go around the people who decide, through a group you lead
wait for the party's pick and back them
say you cannot think about that now
patterns.ifNo: Waiting writes that you waited your turn. The pick owes you a little, and the seat may not open again for years.

sources.life: Appointed to her late husband's Senate seat in 1931, Caraway faced a primary in 1932. Senator Huey Long of Louisiana toured Arkansas with her for a week, partly to gain influence in the home state of a rival, and she won easily.

choices: accept one event, not the tour
patterns.ifNo: Turning it down writes that you refused. You run on your own, and {their rival} hears and comes to you instead.

Problems on her petition, when the record holds them.

You run against an entrenched member for a higher seat and lose badly; the people you knocked off the ballot do not help.

sources.life: In 1995 state senator Alice Palmer backed him to succeed her, then filed to keep her seat. His campaign challenged petitions, and she withdrew after most of her signatures were ruled invalid; he ran unopposed.

patterns.moment: {incumbent}, who endorsed you for her seat, has filed to keep it after all.
choices: challenge her petition before the election board
run against her on the ballot
patterns.ifNo: Stepping aside writes that you kept faith. She owes you, and the seat may open again when she leaves.

your own party's sitting member, whom you filed against

How far your stances are from {incumbent}'s.
Backing from a group outside the party.

The group that recruited you says it will drop you if you take any deal.

branches.when: you stay in and go where {incumbent} never goes
branches.then: A voter asks you to come back after the election, and that promise goes on the record.

sources.life: In 1948 he challenged a fellow Republican, an isolationist congressman, in the primary, campaigning at factory gates, church socials and farms from a Quonset hut, and won.

ask for that promise in writing before you answer
patterns.ifNo: Dropping out writes that you took the deal. {incumbent} is renominated, and the promise becomes a record {party official} has to keep.

patterns.ifNo: Stepping aside writes that you put the friendship first. {friend} may ask you to endorse them.

{the problem} is your first bill, and later scenes read whether it got fixed.

turn it around: how little {incumbent} has done on {the problem}
patterns.ifNo: Saying nothing writes that you stayed on message. That week's doors have read the mailer, and some ask you about it.

your partner or a parent, in the room

Whether you will be able to serve.
The victory plays at the bedside instead of on a stage.

choices: let {household member} speak for you at the final rally
put out a statement from the bed
tell {campaign manager} to keep it quiet
patterns.ifNo: Keeping it quiet is a lie by silence on the record. If a reporter finds out, the story is the secret, not the illness.

a court ruling, a law or a measure on record that redrew districts or switched to district seats

You lost an earlier race.

Weeks later the neighbors who helped meet you, and they are the first of your volunteers.

call your supporters to the next meeting

gates: A vacancy {the body} fills by vote.
You hold a seat on {the body}, or you applied.

branches.then: You speak to {the body} for a few minutes, members question you, and the vote is the outcome.
{member} offers a vote on something you want if you switch, a deal on both records.

branches.when: the seat could have been yours
branches.then: If you turned down a seat that came to you, the one you passed over sits in the room.

sources.life: When a Westbrook, Maine, council seat fell vacant, four residents applied. The first vote ended in a three-way tie; one member changed his vote, and she won the revote.

patterns.moment: {the body} must fill a vacancy, the vote is tied, and {member} backs a different applicant than you.
choices: ask for another round of questions to the applicants
patterns.ifNo: Holding writes that you kept your vote. The tie goes on, and whoever breaks it is owed by the winner.

patterns.title: Your deputy files against you

roles.fill: your top deputy, said with years in the office

setting.text: Where {deputy} would tell you, or where you hear it first.

gates: You hold an office by appointment to finish a term.
{deputy} filed for it.

branches.when: a parent worked in the same office
branches.then: The older staff take sides by family as much as by work.
If the law keeps you in the post until the term ends, you serve for months beside the winner's people.
They stay neutral or back {deputy}, a record you read at the next filing.

sources.life: After about 43 years in LaPorte County, Indiana, election work, she was picked in 2008 to finish the retiring clerk's term, then finished a distant third in the primary to her own top deputy.

patterns.moment: {deputy} has filed for the office you were appointed to finish.
choices: keep {deputy} at their desk through the race
patterns.ifNo: Asking them to withdraw writes that you tried to clear the field. Word reaches the party leaders who picked you.

patterns.title: The senior member sizes you up

roles.fill: the chamber's most powerful senior member, said with the committee and years, from the other wing

setting.text: Where {senior member} would ask you to come.

gates: First term in a legislature.
{senior member} holds power over committees or the calendar.
weights: How far your stances are from theirs.
Traits that are diligent or that charm.

branches.when: you are the first of your kind, or the youngest
branches.then: The room expects you to keep quiet, and a first floor speech changes that.
Months later you are asked to be vice-chair of the committee that draws districts.
You know their bill better than they do and say so politely. They respect it or resent it, by their traits.

sources.life: In 1967 the first Black woman in the Texas Senate won respect by befriending conservatives, among them the chamber's most powerful member, and was named outstanding freshman.
He took his Assembly seat at 23, expected by the old members to keep quiet.

patterns.moment: {senior member} asks you to stop by in your first month and to back them on a procedural vote.
choices: say you will decide on the merits
ask what they can do for your district's bill
patterns.ifNo: Deciding on the merits writes that you kept your distance. Your bills move slower, and they watch how you vote.

patterns.title: Be my running mate

roles.fill: someone the record ties to you as a mentor: teacher, coach, first boss

setting.text: Where {mentor}'s campaign works from.

gates: A mentor tie with someone running for governor.
You hold a seat in the legislature.
weights: How safe your own seat is.

branches.then: The ticket is behind, and you work the small events the top of the ticket skips.
If you win, {mentor} offers you a board to chair, with its own pressures.

sources.life: In 1970 his former teacher and coach, Mike O'Callaghan, ran for governor of Nevada and chose Reid, then a young assemblyman, as his running mate; they won as underdogs.

patterns.moment: {mentor}, now running for governor, asks you onto the ticket.
choices: say you would rather keep your seat
ask what the job would really be
patterns.ifNo: Saying no writes that you turned {mentor} down. They pick someone else, and the tie holds or cools by how you said it.

patterns.title: The apology ad

roles.fill: your media adviser
an unpopular act of yours that the rival used: a fee or tax raised, a program cut

setting.text: Wherever the comeback campaign works from.

gates: You lost reelection as an executive.
{the decision} is on record and the rival used it.
You filed or are weighing a rematch.

branches.then: If you nearly lost your own primary, {ad maker} names it as the first sign you missed.
A friend says people felt you stopped listening. Agreeing changes the ad.

sources.life: He lost reelection as Arkansas governor in 1980 to Frank White, whose ads hit him for raising car license fees. In 1982 he ran ads apologizing and promising to listen, and won.

patterns.moment: A year after losing reelection, {ad maker} brings a draft ad about the decision that cost you.
choices: blame the other government whose decision landed on you (true only if the record shows it)
patterns.ifNo: Refusing to make an ad about it writes that you will not revisit it. The rival's ads still do.

patterns.title: A committee that does not fit your district

roles.fill: a committee whose subject does not match your district's industries and needs
a leader from your district with an idea that fits the committee
a member of the other party on the committee

setting.text: Wherever the community leader would bring the idea to you.

gates: First term in a legislature.
{the committee}'s subject does not match your district's records.
weights: How far the committee is from your district.
Ties with members of the other party.

branches.then: Writing the bill together goes on both records.
The leader says you can if you help in the next leadership vote.
Whether you credit them in public changes their tie.

sources.life: In 1969 the Speaker put her on the Agriculture Committee, which made little sense for Brooklyn. Following a rabbi's idea to use surplus food for the hungry, she worked with Senator Bob Dole to expand food stamps and helped create WIC.

patterns.moment: You were put on {the committee}, which has little to do with your district.
choices: ask the leader to move you
make the committee serve your district
patterns.ifNo: Waiting writes that you accepted the seat. The term passes with little to show on that committee.

patterns.title: The vote for leader

roles.fill: a member running for leader, said with the post they hold
the other, said with theirs

setting.text: Where each would catch you: on the floor, by phone that evening.

gates: You hold a seat in a legislature.
A contest for party leader in the body.

branches.then: You get the committee you wanted, and the leader expects your vote on the first hard bill.
Your committee stays where it was, and the winner's people do not forget.
Standing with a third candidate makes you a name in the body, for better or worse.

sources.life: She moved off the Agriculture Committee to Veterans' Affairs, and later Education and Labor, after voting for Hale Boggs for majority leader.

patterns.moment: {candidate one} and {candidate two} are running to lead your party in the body, and both want your vote.
choices: ask each what they would do for your district
patterns.ifNo: Keeping it private writes nothing either can count on. The winner remembers you did not commit.

patterns.title: The local who knows every door

roles.fill: someone with ties across the district and no campaign, said with where they grew up and what they do

setting.text: Where {local operator} would catch you after you spoke: the back of a hall, the sidewalk outside.

gates: Candidate.
A person on record with ties across the district who is with no campaign.
They attended an event where you spoke.
weights: How far your background is from the district's.

branches.when: they doubted you as a rich outsider
branches.then: They say so first. Whether you answer it decides how hard they work.

branches.when: they complain that politicians never knock
branches.then: They take you door to door on their own streets, which opens doors no list would.
They stay for years, a staff tie later scenes read.

sources.person: John F. Kennedy and Dave Powers
sources.life: In Kennedy's 1946 House race in Boston, Dave Powers, a Charlestown man who knew the district and had doubted a rich Harvard man, joined after hearing him speak to mothers who had lost sons in the war, and stayed with him until 1963.

patterns.moment: {local operator}, who knows the district's families and doubted you, offers to work for you after hearing you speak where you did not expect anyone to listen.
choices: ask them to run your days and your doors
thank them and keep your own people
patterns.ifNo: Keeping your own people writes that you turned them down. They sit out or go to {rival}, and the doors they knew stay closed.

patterns.title: The manager you love

roles.fill: your partner, a sibling or someone you are seeing
a job or client on their record that a rival could use

setting.text: Where you would talk it over: home, the campaign office after hours.

gates: Candidate.
A close recorded tie who has offered to run it.
weights: How much money the campaign has.

branches.when: a sibling with money and connections
branches.then: They pay for it and run it. The campaign is the family's, and the sibling's word carries.

branches.when: their pay is on the reports
branches.then: A reporter asks why your partner is paid what they are.
A client, a foreign government or a lobby job on their record becomes {rival}'s line.

branches.when: a money matter in your own family
branches.then: A family payment that should have gone back to a public program surfaces. Pay it back and call it an error, or fight it.

sources.life: In her 1992 Illinois Senate race she paid her fiancé, Kgosie Matthews, a monthly fee as a strategist, which drew scrutiny. It also came out that part of a timber royalty from family land should have repaid Medicaid for her mother's care; she paid it and called it an error.
Her brother Wellington, a well-connected Montana Republican, financed and managed her 1916 campaign.

patterns.moment: {close tie} wants to run your campaign, and the campaign's people have doubts.
choices: give them the job, with a salary on the reports
give them a role without pay
give them the money side only, as treasurer
keep the campaign to hired staff
patterns.ifNo: Keeping them out writes that you kept the campaign separate. The tie strains or holds, by their traits.

patterns.title: Outspent

roles.fill: a consultant or volunteer with a knack for ads

setting.text: Wherever the campaign works from.

gates: Candidate.
{rival} has raised more than you on the reports.
weights: How far behind in money you are.
How many young volunteers you have.

branches.when: students and first-time voters pour in
branches.then: They want a say in the message, and how you answer keeps them or loses them.
The news plays it for free, and {rival} has to answer it.
The press calls the campaign unserious.

sources.life: Outspent about seven to one by Senator Rudy Boschwitz in Minnesota in 1990, he campaigned from a bus and ran quirky low-budget ads, one a parody in which he goes looking for his opponent. Students and first-time voters joined, and he was the only challenger to beat a sitting senator that year.

patterns.moment: {rival} has many times your money, and {ad maker} pitches something cheap and odd instead of ads you cannot afford.
choices: put the money into a bus and doors instead
ask {donor} to cover the gap, with whatever comes with it
patterns.ifNo: Turning the pitch down writes that you ran a plain campaign, and {rival}'s ads fill the air.

patterns.title: The check you send back

roles.fill: a person or group with business before the office you seek

setting.text: Where the gift reaches you: the mail, a handoff at an event.

gates: Candidate.
A gift on record from someone with business before the office.

branches.then: After several losses you run on handshakes and almost no money, and the papers notice.
In later races you spend almost nothing beyond the filing, and that becomes who you are.

sources.life: He lost three races for governor of Wisconsin before winning the 1957 special Senate election. Late in his career he returned unsolicited donations and spent under $200 to win reelection, mostly on filing paperwork.

patterns.moment: {donor} sends money you did not ask for, and keeping it would make you look like theirs.
choices: send it back with a note
send it back and say so in public
make a rule to take no money at all
patterns.ifNo: Keeping it writes the gift on the reports and a tie with {donor} that a rival or reporter can read.

patterns.title: Every paper against you

roles.fill: whoever runs your message

setting.text: Wherever the campaign works from.

gates: Candidate.
The outlets on record have endorsed {rival}.
weights: How spread out the place is.

branches.then: It becomes a record of what you said that reporters can quote back.

branches.when: the papers run your old words
branches.then: The attacks become a daily box of your own lines.

sources.life: In the 1928 Louisiana governor's race he used sound trucks and radio ads; running for the Senate in 1930 with all of the state's daily papers backing his opponent, he started his own paper.
In the 1934 California governor's race the big Hearst and Chandler papers attacked him throughout.

patterns.moment: Every outlet in {the place} has endorsed {rival}, and {staffer} says the campaign needs its own way to reach people.
choices: start your own paper or sheet
buy radio time or sound trucks
go town to town in person
patterns.ifNo: Going on as before writes that you left the press to {rival}.

patterns.title: The party leaves its own nominee

roles.fill: the county chair of your party
a top appointment you would make, such as the police chief

setting.text: Where {party official} would summon you.

gates: You won your party's nomination.
A party organization on record with a chair.
weights: How much the organization's turnout matters in your place.
How far your stances are from the chair's.

branches.when: the organization backs the other party's candidate
branches.then: The attacks come from your own side, and the outside help they draw is real: money and volunteers from beyond the place.
{party official} is an enemy you face in the next primary.

branches.when: trouble at the polls in your strongest precincts
branches.then: A complaint, a lawyer and a watcher, as in the count that looks wrong.

sources.life: After he beat Gary, Indiana's sitting mayor in the 1967 Democratic primary, the county chairman wanted a say over the police chief and other top posts. Hatcher refused, the organization swung behind the Republican, and its tactics backfired by drawing outside money and help. Hatcher won narrowly.

patterns.moment: You won your party's primary, and {party official} says the organization helps only if it gets a say over {the post}.
choices: give a say over one post
refuse and run without the organization
ask the state or national party to step in
patterns.ifNo: Giving in writes an obligation {party official} calls in once you hold office.

patterns.title: The visit that goes wrong

roles.fill: whoever holds an office with reach in that world, said with the office
a place where voters who oppose you gather: a church, a market, a hall, from the record

setting.text: {the stop}, chosen from where opposition to you is strongest on the record.

gates: Candidate.
A visit by {powerful officeholder} on the calendar.
A stop in an area that opposes you.

branches.then: It can reach voters put off by the crowd. Using it writes an ad record and costs you the stop's voters for good.
They say you chose the stop, and the next visit is harder to get.

sources.life: In the 1983 Chicago general election, protesters confronted Washington and former Vice President Walter Mondale outside St. Pascal's church on the Northwest Side. The campaign later used footage of them in ads aimed at white liberals.

patterns.moment: {powerful officeholder} came to campaign beside you, and at {the stop} the crowd turns on you both.
choices: use the footage of the crowd in an ad
patterns.ifNo: Leaving writes that you left. The footage runs without your answer.

patterns.title: The rival who coasts

roles.fill: the front-runner

setting.text: Wherever the news reaches you.

gates: Candidate.
A remark or an absence on {rival}'s record.

branches.then: That person backs you.

branches.when: you are the one far ahead
branches.then: The days off and the remark are yours to take or not, and the record keeps where you were.

sources.life: In the January 2010 Massachusetts special Senate election, Democrat Martha Coakley took days off less than a month out, asked whether she should be standing outside Fenway Park shaking hands, and called the pitcher Curt Schilling a Yankees fan. Brown, a Republican, won.

patterns.moment: {rival}, far ahead, takes days off and says something that sounds like the race is beneath them.
choices: go where {rival} will not: the stadium gate, the plant at shift change
put the remark in an ad
say nothing and keep working the district
ask whoever {rival} slighted for an endorsement
patterns.ifNo: Saying nothing writes nothing. {rival}'s lead holds or slips on its own.

patterns.title: The machine against you

roles.fill: the long-serving executive you are running against
whoever runs your field work

setting.text: Wherever the campaign works from, the morning after.

gates: Candidate against a sitting executive.
Workers or police on record pulling signs or pressuring staff (acts by people in the world, never authored).
weights: How many public workers live in your district.

branches.then: The run-again question comes the morning after.

branches.when: a film crew follows the campaign
branches.then: What they catch becomes a record later scenes read.

sources.life: Challenging Newark's longtime mayor Sharpe James in 2002, he was called a carpetbagger and too suburban to understand the city, and a documentary showed police and firefighters tearing down a big Booker sign. He lost about 53 to 47 and won in 2006.

patterns.moment: Your signs come down overnight, and {staffer} says people who work for {the place} are being told not to help you.
choices: put the signs back up every night
film it and go to the press
answer the not-one-of-us charge at the doors
patterns.ifNo: Letting it go writes nothing filed, and the doors go quieter.

patterns.title: The rival under indictment

roles.fill: the sitting holder, with charges on the justice record

setting.text: Wherever the campaign works from.

gates: Candidate of the party that does not hold the seat.
Charges against {incumbent} on the justice record.
weights: How far along the case is.

branches.then: A disaster on record pushes the dates back under the state's election law, and the trial now falls near the vote.
You campaign from a damaged house, and voters see it.

sources.life: In 2008 the nine-term New Orleans congressman William Jefferson was under federal indictment. Hurricane Gustav pushed the election back, and Cao, a Republican whose own home flooded in the storm, won a heavily Democratic seat.

patterns.moment: {incumbent} is under indictment, and you are the other party's long shot in a seat your party never wins.
choices: run on what the district needs
stay quiet and let the trial speak
patterns.ifNo: Staying quiet writes that you did not make the charges your campaign.

patterns.title: Where were you

roles.fill: the sitting member, with absences or paid speeches on record
your ad maker

setting.text: Wherever the campaign works from.

gates: Candidate against an incumbent.
{incumbent}'s absences or paid speeches on record.

branches.then: The ad overstates it and is marked as a lie. Anyone can find the true figure.
Answer with your record, ignore it, or hit back.

sources.life: In the 1984 Kentucky Senate race his ads showed bloodhounds searching for Senator Dee Huddleston over missed votes and paid speeches. Huddleston's voting record was in fact high, and McConnell won by about 5,000 votes.

patterns.moment: {ad maker} has an ad that hunts for {incumbent} over missed votes and paid speeches.
choices: run it with the true attendance figure in it
patterns.ifNo: Refusing writes that you kept it off the air.

patterns.title: Not one of us

roles.fill: your opponent

setting.text: Where the charge reaches you: a forum, an ad, a door.

gates: Candidate.
A fact on your record the charge can stand on: schooling elsewhere, a recent move, family money.
weights: How far your background is from the district's.

branches.then: The answer is the service, said once at a forum, and it ends the charge.

branches.when: you were away at school, from money
branches.then: {rival} sets your school beside theirs, and it sticks unless you have something local to point to.
You never let yourself be outdone on roots again, a stance later scenes read.

sources.life: Running for an open West Texas House seat in 1978, he was painted by Democrat Kent Hance as out of touch with rural Texans. He lost, the only race he ever lost.
A newcomer to Arizona accused of carpetbagging in 1982, he answered at a candidates' forum that the longest he had lived anywhere was Hanoi, as a prisoner of war. He won.

patterns.moment: {rival} says you are not really from here: your schooling, your money or the years you lived elsewhere.
choices: answer with where you were and why
patterns.ifNo: Letting it go writes no answer, and voters who heard it keep it.

patterns.title: Wear the insult

roles.fill: a powerful figure backing {rival}
whoever runs your message

setting.text: Where you would answer it in public: a rally, a broadcast.

gates: Candidate.
A name or insult from {rival}'s side on record.

branches.then: It is yours for every race after, and the press asks about it.
People think you are mocking them.

sources.life: In his 1948 Tennessee Senate race, Memphis boss E. H. Crump's side likened him to a raccoon. Kefauver answered in a coonskin cap, saying he might be a pet coon but not Crump's, won, and kept the cap as his trademark.

patterns.moment: {boss} calls you a name meant to stick, and {staffer} hands you a way to wear it.
choices: answer with a line that turns it around
patterns.ifNo: Ignoring it writes no answer, and the name belongs to {rival}'s side.

patterns.title: Your past comes out

roles.fill: a membership or act from years back on your record

setting.text: Where the press would find you that day.

gates: Candidate.
{the old act} is on your record and a rival can find it.

branches.then: A letter in your own hand shows more than you said. A denial now is a caught lie.

branches.when: you call it the worst mistake of your life
branches.then: The line goes on your record and follows you.

sources.life: In his first House race in West Virginia in 1952, a primary opponent revealed his past Ku Klux Klan membership. Byrd said he had joined in the early 1940s and left; his Republican opponent later found a 1946 letter from Byrd to the Klan's leader. He won, and years later called joining the worst mistake of his life.

patterns.moment: {rival} tells the press about {the old act}.
choices: own it and say why you left
play it down (a lie if the record says more)
go on the air about it
patterns.ifNo: Saying nothing writes that you did not answer, and the story runs its course.

patterns.title: Your own words, cut up

roles.fill: books, columns, posts or old speeches on your record

setting.text: Wherever the campaign works from.

gates: Candidate.
A body of writing or speeches on your record.

branches.then: A big employer docks pay or presses staff to give to {rival}, and a worker tells you.
Filmed voter interviews against you turn out to use actors, and exposing it is a press story.

sources.life: Running for California governor in 1934, he was hit with out-of-context quotes from his own novels run daily in the papers, and with newsreels of staged voter interviews; studio heads pressured employees to give to his opponent. He lost.

patterns.moment: {rival}'s side runs lines from {your writing}, cut from their context, every day.
choices: say the words were a character's, not yours
patterns.ifNo: Ignoring it writes no answer, and the quotes become what people think you said.

patterns.title: The attack on your partner

roles.fill: a paper or station on record
your partner

setting.text: Where you would answer: the outlet's door, a statement, your own front steps.

gates: Candidate.
An attack on {household member} on the press record.

branches.then: The press says you cried, or that it was melting snow, and the story becomes your composure.

branches.when: the letter behind it was forged
branches.then: Later it comes out that a rival campaign planted it. The lie is theirs on the record.

branches.when: you win by less than expected
branches.then: The margin reads as a loss.

sources.life: Two weeks before the 1972 New Hampshire primary, the Manchester Union Leader ran a letter accusing him of laughing at a slur and an editorial attacking his wife. He answered outside the paper's offices in the snow, and reporters wrote that he cried, which he denied. The letter was later tied to the Nixon campaign's dirty tricks.

patterns.moment: {outlet} has attacked {household member} in print, days before the vote.
choices: answer it in public, at the outlet's door
patterns.ifNo: Saying nothing writes that you let it stand.

patterns.title: The letter in the last week

roles.fill: your faith, your marriage, or a false charge against you

setting.text: Wherever it reaches you.

gates: Candidate, in the final week.
A letter or flyer on record.

branches.then: {rival} disowns it or does not, and both are records.
Answering gives it air; not answering lets it spread.

sources.life: Late in his 1990 race, a letter from his opponent's supporters attacked him for marrying a non-Jew, and Wellstone fired back.
In the 1983 Chicago race a flier made a false criminal accusation against him.

patterns.moment: In the final week, a letter or flyer goes around about {the target}.
patterns.ifNo: Ignoring it writes no answer.

patterns.title: Your name is the only reason

roles.fill: a well-known officeholder in your family

setting.text: the debate stage, because the line is said in front of everyone.

gates: Candidate in a debate.
{your relative} is on your record.

branches.then: Your aide steers you out of the hall before you do anything.
People who listened think {rival} won; people who watched think you did.

branches.when: the line makes you the underdog
branches.then: A supporter says {rival} made a rich candidate the underdog.

sources.life: In a South Boston debate for the 1962 Massachusetts Senate primary, Edward McCormack said Kennedy's candidacy would be a joke if his name were Edward Moore. Kennedy's voice reportedly shook in his closing, an aide steered him out afterward, and he won the primary by more than two to one.

patterns.moment: On the debate stage, {rival} says that without your family's name your run would be a joke.
choices: answer with what you have done yourself
let it pass and give your closing
hit back at {rival}'s own family ties
lose your temper (only with the traits for it)
patterns.ifNo: Letting it pass writes that you took it. How it reads depends on who watched and who listened.

patterns.title: Who gets on the stage

roles.fill: the moderator, said with the outlet that set up the debate

setting.text: the debate hall, because the stage is what is being fought over.

gates: Candidate.
A debate on the calendar that your campaign paid for.
weights: How far ahead or behind you are.

branches.when: you are the one left out
branches.then: You stand at the edge of the stage, and leaving quietly or speaking up is the scene.

branches.when: {rival} refuses to go on with the others
branches.then: {rival} looks small or principled, by the room.

sources.life: Before the 1980 New Hampshire primary he paid for a debate a Nashua paper set up with George H. W. Bush and invited the other candidates. Bush refused to debate with them, the moderator ordered Reagan's microphone cut, and Reagan said he was paying for it. He won the primary easily.

patterns.moment: You paid for the debate and brought the other candidates, and {moderator} orders your microphone cut.
choices: insist you are paying for it
go along with the two-person format
walk off with the candidates who were left out
patterns.ifNo: Going along writes that you took the sponsor's format, and the left-out candidates remember.

patterns.title: The comparison

roles.fill: a revered officeholder from the world's own history
an opponent on record with a tie to {the figure}

setting.text: the debate stage.

gates: Candidate in a debate.
{the figure} is in the world's history, and {rival}'s tie to them is on record.

branches.then: The warning is on record, and making it anyway is your choice.

branches.when: you are the one who knew them
branches.then: Deliver the rebuke, or let it go.

branches.when: you lose the exchange and win the race
branches.then: The line follows you anyway.

sources.life: Pressed on experience in the 1988 vice-presidential debate, Quayle compared his time in Congress to John F. Kennedy's. Bentsen, who had known Kennedy, told him he was no Jack Kennedy. Quayle's advisers had warned him, and the ticket won anyway.

patterns.moment: You might compare yourself on stage to {the figure}, and {rival} knew them.
choices: prepare an answer in case it comes up
patterns.ifNo: Leaving it out writes nothing.

patterns.title: Under the lights

roles.fill: whoever handles the broadcast

setting.text: Where you get ready before the broadcast.

gates: Candidate.
A televised debate on the calendar.
weights: How tired you are on the record.

branches.then: You look pale under the lights, and people talk about how you looked more than what you said.
They look fresh, and the comparison is made for you.
The papers argue for weeks about whether it mattered.

sources.person: John F. Kennedy and Richard Nixon
sources.life: Before the first televised debate in 1960, Nixon had been ill and hurt his knee and looked pale in a gray suit that blended into the set; accounts differ on his makeup. Kennedy had practiced and rested. The claim that radio listeners judged it differently rests on thin polling.

patterns.moment: The first televised debate is tonight, and {staffer} asks how you want to look.
choices: change your clothes for the set
patterns.ifNo: Going on as you are writes nothing. The camera decides.

patterns.title: The first spots

roles.fill: an advertising man or consultant

setting.text: Where the spots are filmed: a studio, an office made up for it.

gates: Candidate.
An ad budget on the reports.

branches.when: the voters are recruited off the street
branches.then: They are filmed apart from you, looking up as if at you, and a reporter can find out.
Their reach falls behind yours.

sources.life: In 1952 adman Rosser Reeves persuaded him that short spots placed near shows like I Love Lucy would reach more people than long speeches. Eisenhower read answers from cue cards to questions from tourists filmed separately. Adlai Stevenson refused to appear in his own TV ads.

patterns.moment: {ad maker} wants you to read short answers to ordinary voters' questions, filmed apart from them, to run between popular shows.
choices: do them only with real voters in the room
patterns.ifNo: Refusing writes that you would not be sold like soap, and {rival}'s spots run.

patterns.title: The line on every sign

roles.fill: whoever runs your message

setting.text: Wherever the campaign works from.

gates: Candidate.
weights: How well the line fits your record.

branches.when: the line plays on who you are
branches.then: It works where people already see you that way and costs you where they do not.
A hat, a color or a cap becomes yours.
The line becomes a target.

sources.life: Running against a 14-year incumbent in a 1970 Manhattan Democratic primary, she used the slogan that a woman's place is in the House, the House of Representatives, was known for her hats, and won.

patterns.moment: {staffer} wants one line for every sign and ad, and the pick is yours.
choices: a line built from your own record and who you are (four drawn from it)
patterns.ifNo: Just your name writes a plain campaign. Doors and ads carry no message.

patterns.title: Nobody sent you

roles.fill: the party's ward or district office
the party's man for the ward, said with the post

setting.text: {the party office}, because the door is the moment.

gates: Not in office.
{the party office} is on record in your area.
weights: Your ties to anyone in the party.
How closed the local party is.

branches.then: The name opens the door, and you owe the name.

branches.when: you go to the reform side
branches.then: The faction tie is the start of your career.

sources.life: In 1948 he walked into his Chicago ward office to volunteer for Adlai Stevenson and Paul Douglas. Asked who sent him, he said nobody, and was turned away; he later called it the start of his political career.

patterns.moment: You offer to volunteer at {the party office}, and {committeeman} asks who sent you.
choices: leave and find another way in: a reform club, an independent group
come back with someone who vouches for you
patterns.ifNo: Leaving writes that the party turned you away. Another group may find you.

patterns.title: Register them first

roles.fill: someone who runs house meetings and registration drives

setting.text: Where {organizer} would find you: after a meeting they ran, at your door.

gates: Adults who are not registered live in a part of your district that would back you, by the voter roll.

branches.then: The drive is your answer to the loss.
The groups that join expect their share after the win.

sources.life: After he lost a Los Angeles council race in 1947, the Community Service Organization he helped found, with organizer Fred Ross holding house meetings, registered about 15,000 new voters in Boyle Heights. With labor and Jewish voters behind him, he won in 1949.

patterns.moment: {organizer} says the people who would vote for you are not registered, and asks for months before you run.
choices: spend months registering voters before you run
run now with who is registered
join with labor and other groups to share the work
patterns.ifNo: Running now writes that you ran on the rolls as they were.

patterns.title: Go where people already are

roles.fill: whoever runs your schedule

setting.text: Wherever the campaign plans its week.

gates: Candidate.
The district's places are on record.
weights: How spread out the district is.
Ties from a cause you worked for.

branches.then: People you worked with before turn out and host you.
The family's ties set the stops.

sources.life: Running statewide in Montana in 1916, she spoke at train stations, street corners, potlucks and one-room schools, drawing on the network from her suffrage campaigns, and became the first woman elected to Congress.

patterns.moment: Your district is wide and thinly settled, and {staffer} asks where next week's stops go.
choices: where crowds already gather: the station, a supper, a school event
where your network from an earlier cause lives
patterns.ifNo: Staying in the towns writes that the far places never saw you.

patterns.title: The volunteer who wants a real job

roles.fill: a volunteer on record with weeks of work

setting.text: Wherever the campaign works from.

gates: Candidate.
{volunteer}'s work is on record.

branches.when: many of your volunteers are parents
branches.then: Child care at the office changes who can come.
They come back to ask for your endorsement.

sources.life: Her 1970 campaign office offered free drop-in child care, and she pushed to promote women from canvassers into staff jobs.

patterns.moment: {volunteer}, who has knocked doors for weeks, asks for a staff job over a hired professional.
choices: set up child care at the office so parents can volunteer
patterns.ifNo: Keeping roles writes that you kept them a volunteer, and they may drift away.

patterns.title: Follow me around

roles.fill: a reporter, said with the outlet
something in your household record a reporter could learn

setting.text: Where {reporter} would confront you: outside your home, by your car.

gates: Candidate.
{the private fact} is on your record and a reporter could learn it.
weights: Whether you dared reporters to follow you.

branches.when: you told reporters to follow you
branches.then: They did, and the remark is quoted back.
Months later you return, and the first question is the old one.

sources.life: In 1987 he told a reporter that anyone who wanted could follow him around. The Miami Herald acted on a tip, watched his townhouse and confronted him, and he suspended his campaign within days.

patterns.moment: {reporter} asks about {the private fact} after a tip, and says they watched your home.
patterns.ifNo: Refusing writes that you would not answer, and the story runs without you.

patterns.title: A line of your own

roles.fill: whoever runs your effort

setting.text: Wherever the effort meets.

gates: Candidate not nominated by a major party.
weights: How unpopular the major parties are on record.
How many candidates split the vote.

branches.when: the state will not list your party
branches.then: You sue to get it listed.
You win with a plurality, and the record says how few chose you.

branches.when: reformers of both parties back a fusion ticket
branches.then: Each expects its share after the win.

sources.life: A Socialist Alternative candidate, she sued the state to list her party on the 2012 ballot, lost that race, and in 2013 beat a long-serving Seattle council member on a $15 minimum wage platform.
He ran for New York mayor in 1933 on a Fusion ticket backed by reformers, Republicans and anti-Tammany Democrats, and won.
He left the Republicans and won the 1990 Connecticut governor's race on his own A Connecticut Party line with about 40 percent in a three-way race.

patterns.moment: Neither big party will nominate you, and {organizer} asks how you get on the ballot.
choices: run on a small party's line, suing if it is kept off
run on a fusion line with reformers of both parties
patterns.ifNo: Staying out writes that you did not run. Your backers find someone else.

patterns.title: Ahead at eleven

roles.fill: your manager, with the count

setting.text: Where you watch the returns: headquarters, a hotel, home.

gates: Election night.
Ballots still out on the count record: absentees, late counties.

branches.then: The claim is on record, the press replays it, and conceding weeks later reads worse.
Concede now or wait; the late ballots may be yours.

branches.when: the morning paper names the wrong winner
branches.then: An early edition called it for the loser, and holding it up is the morning's picture.

sources.life: In California's 2010 attorney general race, Republican Cooley declared victory on election night. Ballots counted afterward flipped the race, the lead swung for about three weeks, and he conceded to Harris.
Some outlets projected him the winner of California's 1982 governor's race early in the night; once absentee ballots were counted he lost narrowly.
In 1948 an early edition of the Chicago Daily Tribune declared him the winner, and Harry Truman held up a copy for photographers.

patterns.moment: Early returns have you or {rival} ahead, and {campaign manager} says many ballots are still out.
choices: say every ballot counts and wait
patterns.ifNo: Waiting writes no claim, so there is nothing to take back.

patterns.title: The tie

roles.fill: the election official who runs the drawing

setting.text: wherever the law holds the drawing, because the draw is the moment.

gates: A tie on the count record.
The state's or place's tie law.
weights: What rides on the seat, such as control of the body.

branches.then: The recount puts you ahead by one; a court then counts a disputed ballot and it is tied.

branches.when: control of the body rides on it
branches.then: The leaders of both parties call you.
{clerk} picks the game of chance, beads, dice or a coin, and both sides must accept it.
The official canvass after a coin toss shows one side ahead, and the toss means nothing.

sources.life: A 2017 recount for a Virginia House seat put Democrat Simonds ahead by one vote. A court panel then counted a disputed ballot for Republican Yancey, making a tie; his name was drawn from a bowl, keeping a Republican majority.
A tied 2024 Corpus Christi council runoff was settled in 2025 by drawing numbered beads, after a roll of a die set the order.
A tied 2018 council race was settled by a coin toss; the official canvass then showed the incumbent ahead.

patterns.moment: After the recount and the court, the race is tied, and the law says the winner is drawn by lot.
choices: challenge the disputed ballot in court
patterns.ifNo: Conceding before the draw writes that you gave up the seat.

patterns.title: The long count

roles.fill: your lawyer

setting.text: Where you hear the count: headquarters, a call from {lawyer}.

gates: A margin inside the recount rule on the count record.

branches.then: Months late, colleagues walk you in, and the oath is done twice so your family can stand with you.
A concession after months reads differently from one on the night.

sources.life: Minnesota's 2008 Senate race went through a recount and a court contest for eight months. The state supreme court ruled for Franken by 312 votes, Coleman conceded, and Franken was sworn in that July, escorted by Amy Klobuchar and Walter Mondale.

patterns.moment: The margin is a few hundred votes, the recount and the court fight will take months, and the seat sits empty.
patterns.ifNo: Conceding writes it, and {rival} is sworn in.

patterns.title: Write me in

roles.fill: your closest adviser

setting.text: Where you take the news of the primary loss.

gates: You lost your party's primary.
The state allows write-ins.
weights: How well known your name is.

branches.then: The campaign's doors and ads are about how to write your name.
{rival}'s observers challenge each misspelled ballot, and the election official decides which count.
You are the first in years to win this way, and the party that dropped you has to deal with you.

sources.life: After losing Alaska's 2010 Republican primary to Joe Miller, she ran as a write-in, taught voters to spell her name, and won. At the hand count Miller's observers challenged ballots over spelling, even a cursive letter, and the elections director made the calls.

patterns.moment: You lost the primary, and {staffer} asks whether you run anyway as a write-in.
patterns.ifNo: Conceding writes it, and the nominee expects your endorsement.

patterns.title: The concession call

roles.fill: the candidate who won
your campaign chair, who can speak for you

setting.text: Where you watch the returns, with the people who worked for you.

gates: Election night.
The count record shows you behind.

branches.when: the margin collapses after you called
branches.then: You call back and take it back, after the other side has begun to celebrate.

branches.when: you call in private and speak in the morning
branches.then: The crowd goes home without you, and the next day's speech is the concession on record.

branches.when: you are the winner taking the call
branches.then: Take the concession graciously, or snap when it is taken back.

sources.life: On election night 2000, after the networks called Florida for George W. Bush, Gore phoned Bush to concede, then, as the margin shrank, called back to take it back. His campaign chairman told the crowd the race was too close to call.
In 2016 her campaign chairman told the crowd to go home; she called the winner that night and gave her concession speech the next morning.

patterns.moment: The count says you lost, and {campaign manager} holds the phone: call {winner} now, later, or not yet.
choices: call to concede now (the call follows its real form)
send {chairman} to tell the crowd to go home
speak to the crowd yourself tonight
patterns.ifNo: Not calling writes no concession, and the press asks why.

patterns.title: The crowd boos the winner

roles.fill: the candidate who beat you

setting.text: Where your supporters gathered for the night.

gates: You conceded.
A speech to your supporters that night.

branches.then: The fireworks bought for it are never set off, and the empty lawn is the picture.
It is the record {winner}'s people read when you next need them.

sources.life: In his 2008 concession in Phoenix, some supporters booed when he said he had called Barack Obama, and at a mention of Joe Biden; applause rose when he praised the historic nature of Obama's win.

patterns.moment: In your concession speech, your supporters boo when you say {winner}'s name.
choices: quiet them and say the name again
let it pass and go on
patterns.ifNo: Letting it pass writes the speech as heard with the boos in it, a record {winner}'s people and the press read.

patterns.title: The night you lose the first round

roles.fill: the people who came to work for you

setting.text: Where the campaign gathered for the night.

gates: Candidate.
You lost the first round of a primary or caucus on the calendar.

branches.then: A microphone catches your voice and not the crowd's, and the yell at the end replays for days.
The next contest reads tonight.

sources.life: After finishing third in Iowa in 2004, he spoke to thousands of supporters and ended with a yell. A directional microphone cut out the crowd's noise, and the clip aired hundreds of times within days. He left the race in February.

patterns.moment: You finished far behind in the first contest, and the volunteers who came from everywhere wait for you to speak.
choices: rally them on to the next contest (a speech built one part at a time)
patterns.ifNo: Thanking them quietly writes the speech as heard, and some volunteers lapse on the campaign's record.

patterns.title: Your manager's boast

roles.fill: the manager who ran your race

setting.text: Where the story reaches you the next morning.

gates: You won.
{campaign manager}'s statement is on the press record.
weights: Whether the record holds any such payment.

branches.then: {campaign manager} recants under oath, calling it a story told to needle the other side. The lie is on their record.
Staff told groups the campaign would be ahead if they stayed out. It is on record and can be found.
Their leaders demand an apology and ask you to meet.

sources.person: Christine Todd Whitman and Ed Rollins
sources.life: Days after she won New Jersey's governorship in 1993, her campaign manager told reporters the campaign had paid to keep Black ministers and Democratic workers from turning out voters. He soon called it an exaggeration and later told lawyers under oath it was made up; Black ministers demanded an apology.

patterns.moment: Days after you won, {campaign manager} told reporters the campaign paid people not to turn out voters for {rival}.
choices: disown it and let them go
say it is false and keep them
patterns.ifNo: Saying nothing writes that you let it stand, and the groups it insulted ask why.

patterns.title: The bills after the race

roles.fill: the campaign's treasurer

setting.text: Where the campaign's books are kept.

gates: The campaign ended in debt on its reports.

branches.when: you take a post that bars you from raising money
branches.then: A relative or ally has to raise it for you.
They wait longest for their money, and they talk.

sources.life: She left the 2008 primary about $22.5 million in debt, millions of it her own loans, which she wrote off. As secretary of state she could not raise money herself, so Bill Clinton raised it; her pollster was paid last, and the debt was cleared in 2013.

patterns.moment: The race is over, the campaign owes vendors, staff and you, and {treasurer} asks who gets paid first.
choices: write off what you lent it
keep raising money to pay the vendors
rent the donor list to another campaign
patterns.ifNo: Letting the debt sit writes unpaid vendors who talk, and the reports show it each quarter.

patterns.title: Everyone wants the credit

roles.fill: the groups in your coalition on record: a union, a party faction, reformers, a neighborhood's organizers

setting.text: Wherever the calls reach you that morning.

gates: You won.
Backing from more than one group on record.
weights: How much each group's turnout mattered in the precinct results.

branches.then: Each side expects jobs, and giving to one costs the other.
Their organizers want a seat at the table.

sources.life: He won New York's mayoralty in 1933 with reform Democrats, Republicans, Socialists, and Jewish and most Italian voters, and once in office pushed Tammany appointees out.
In 1949 a coalition of newly registered Mexican American voters, Jewish voters and labor elected him to the Los Angeles council.

patterns.moment: The morning after you win, each group that backed you calls to say it won the race, and what it wants.
choices: ask each what it most needs
patterns.ifNo: Promising nothing writes no obligation. The groups wait, and the first to feel slighted says so.

patterns.title: Run again

roles.fill: your partner, a parent or your oldest friend

setting.text: Wherever you talk the next morning.

gates: You lost a race.
weights: How many times you have lost.

branches.then: The next try comes as a special election, and the papers call you the one who never quits.

branches.when: the incumbent who beat you retires
branches.then: The next run is against someone else.

sources.life: He lost three Wisconsin governor's races, then won the 1957 special Senate election.
He lost the 2002 Newark mayoral race and won in 2006, when the incumbent did not run.
She lost a 2012 state house race to the speaker, then won a Seattle council seat in 2013.

patterns.moment: You lost again, and {close tie} asks whether you will run next time.
choices: run again for the same office
patterns.ifNo: Saying you are done writes it, and the people who worked for you go elsewhere.

patterns.title: The oath

roles.fill: the person who gives the oath, said with the post
the book you swear on, or none

setting.text: where the oath is given, because the oath has its form.

gates: You won, and the oath is on the calendar.
weights: How unusual what you bring is in that body.

branches.then: You cannot raise the hand everyone is told to raise, so you raise the other, and the room goes quiet.
You ask for a book that means something to you. A member of the body tells voters he never would, and your answer is a record.

branches.when: a senior figure jokes about you
branches.then: Laugh, answer or let it pass. That figure later steers your committee.

sources.life: Sworn in as Hawaii's first representative in 1959 and asked to raise his right hand, he raised his left, having lost his right arm in the war. A colleague later said prejudice fell away in that moment.
The first Muslim in Congress took a ceremonial oath in 2007 on Thomas Jefferson's Quran, after a congressman wrote to voters criticizing the choice.
He was sworn in in 2009 on a Bible from the Wellstone family, and the oath was redone in the old chamber so his family could stand with him.

patterns.moment: {official} gives you the oath in its real form, and something about you is not the usual.
choices: which book, or an affirmation without one
a second ceremonial oath for your family
how to answer a critic of your choice
patterns.ifNo: Taking the plain form writes nothing extra, and a critic has nothing to say.

patterns.title: Nobody walks you in

roles.fill: the senior member from your state or place, with a grudge on record
a member from somewhere else

setting.text: the chamber floor, because the walk happens in front of everyone.

gates: You are being sworn in.
A custom of escort on record.
A grudge between you and {senior member} on record.

branches.when: the grudge goes back to a race
branches.then: You backed someone else against him once, and the record says why.
A tie, and a debt later votes read.

sources.life: When he came to take his Senate seat in 1875, Mississippi's senior senator, James Alcorn, refused to escort him and kept reading a newspaper. Roscoe Conkling of New York crossed the chamber and walked with him.

patterns.moment: Custom says {senior member} walks you to the oath, and he stays in his seat, reading.
choices: take {stranger}'s arm when he crosses the floor
patterns.ifNo: Walking alone writes nothing owed to anyone.

patterns.title: They will not seat you

roles.fill: a statement you made, a question about your citizenship or residence, or a complaint about how your election was run

setting.text: Where the vote happens, and where you hear it.

gates: You won.
A challenge to your seat on record.
weights: How many members are against you.

branches.then: The highest court rules unanimously that views cannot bar you, and you take the seat late.
Your papers were never finished, and {the body} votes you out.
You are one of several, and {the body} votes on all at once.

sources.life: In 1966 the Georgia House kept him out over his statements against the Vietnam War. The Supreme Court ruled unanimously that a legislator's views cannot disqualify him, and he was seated.
In 1880 the California Senate voted to disqualify him after it came out that he had never completed his citizenship.
A New York congressman objected to seating Mississippi's members over the denial of Black voters' rights. The House seated them after a vote.

patterns.moment: {the body} votes not to seat you over {the challenge}.
